Algebra · algebraic fractions

Simplifying algebraic fractions (Higher)

  • An algebraic fraction has algebra in the numerator, the denominator or both.
  • To simplify, factorise the numerator and denominator fully, then cancel common factors (whole brackets or whole factors).
  • x2−5x+6x2−2x​=(x−3)(x−2)x(x−2)​=x−3x​(x² − 2x)/(x² − 5x + 6) = (x(x − 2))/((x − 3)(x − 2)) = x/(x − 3)
  • You can only cancel factors, never single terms: in xx+3​(x + 3)/x nothing cancels.
Quick check
?Simplify fully 4x2−92x2+3x​(2x² + 3x)/(4x² − 9).
Algebra · algebraic fractions

The four operations with algebraic fractions (Higher)

  • Multiply: factorise, cancel, then multiply numerators and denominators.
  • Divide: flip the second fraction and multiply: 43a​÷109a​=43a​×9a10​=65​3a/4 ÷ 9a/10 = 3a/4 × 10/9a = 5/6.
  • Add or subtract: use a common denominator, just as 21​+31​=63+2​1/2 + 1/3 = (3 + 2)/6.
  • x1​+x+11​=x(x+1)(x+1)+x​=x(x+1)2x+1​1/x + 1/(x + 1) = ((x + 1) + x)/(x(x + 1)) = (2x + 1)/(x(x + 1))
  • Never add the denominators: 21​+31​1/2 + 1/3 is not 52​2/5.
Calculate
?Write x2​+x+13​2/x + 3/(x + 1) as a single fraction x(x+1)ax+b​(ax + b)/(x(x + 1)). Enter the value of aa (exact).
Worked example Algebra · algebraic fractions

Subtracting algebraic fractions (Higher)

Question
Write x+23x+1​−x−1x−2​(3x + 1)/(x + 2) − (x − 2)/(x − 1) as a single fraction.
  1. 1
    Use the common denominator (x+2)(x−1)(x + 2)(x − 1): (x+2)(x−1)(3x+1)(x−1)−(x−2)(x+2)​((3x + 1)(x − 1) − (x − 2)(x + 2))/((x + 2)(x − 1))
  2. 2
    Expand the first product: (3x+1)(x−1)=3x2−2x−1(3x + 1)(x − 1) = 3x² − 2x − 1
  3. 3
    Expand the second product: (x−2)(x+2)=x2−4(x − 2)(x + 2) = x² − 4
  4. 4
    Subtract the whole second product: 3x2−2x−1−(x2−4)=2x2−2x+33x² − 2x − 1 − (x² − 4) = 2x² − 2x + 3
Answer
(x+2)(x−1)2x2−2x+3​(2x² − 2x + 3)/((x + 2)(x − 1))
⚠️ Watch out
the minus applies to all of x2−4x² − 4, so −(−4)=+4−(−4) = +4. Writing −x2−4−x² − 4 gives the wrong numerator 2x2−2x−52x² − 2x − 5.
Worked example Algebra · algebraic fractions

Solving an equation with algebraic fractions (Higher)

Question
Solve x+22​+2x−13​=12/(x + 2) + 3/(2x − 1) = 1.
  1. 1
    Multiply every term by (x+2)(2x−1)(x + 2)(2x − 1): 2(2x−1)+3(x+2)=(x+2)(2x−1)2(2x − 1) + 3(x + 2) = (x + 2)(2x − 1)
  2. 2
    Expand both sides: 7x+4=2x2+3x−27x + 4 = 2x² + 3x − 2
  3. 3
    Rearrange to =0= 0: 2x2−4x−6=02x² − 4x − 6 = 0, so x2−2x−3=0x² − 2x − 3 = 0
  4. 4
    Factorise: (x−3)(x+1)=0(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0
  5. 5
    Check neither value makes a denominator zero: both are fine
Answer
x=3x = 3 or x=−1x = −1
⚠️ Watch out
multiply every term, including the 1 on the right, by the common denominator.
Calculate
?A walker goes 12 km uphill at xx km/h, then 12 km back down at (x+2)(x + 2) km/h. The whole walk takes 5 hours. Form an equation and solve it to find the uphill speed (exact).
km/h
Calculate
?Some equations have no simple method of solving, so you use trial and improvement: try a value, see if the answer is too big or too small, and narrow it down. x3−2x=30x³ − 2x = 30 has a solution between 3 and 4. Use trial and improvement to find it to 1 decimal place.
Mission check

?Cycle a route at 10 km/h and ride back along it at 30 km/h. What is your average speed for the whole trip?

Time is distance ÷ speed, so the two legs take 10d​d/10 and 30d​d/30 hours, a total of 303d+d​=152d​(3d + d)/30 = 2d/15. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time =2d÷152d​=15= 2d ÷ 2d/15 = 15 km/h, whatever the distance. The slow leg takes longer, so it drags the average below 20.

Algebra · circles on a grid

The equation of a circle (Higher)

  • A point (x,y)(x, y) on a circle with centre the origin and radius rr makes a right-angled triangle with legs xx and yy.
  • By Pythagoras, every point on the circle satisfies
x2+y2=r2x² + y² = r²
  • x2+y2=25x² + y² = 25 has radius 5: (3,4)(3, 4) is on it because 9+16=259 + 16 = 25.
  • If x2+y2<r2x² + y² < r² the point is inside; if x2+y2>r2x² + y² > r² it is outside.

Finding a missing coordinate (Higher)

The point (p,4)(p, 4) lies on the circle x2+y2=41x² + y² = 41, and p<0p < 0. Find pp.

  3. 3

the square root has two signs. Read the question to choose the right one.

?Is each point inside, on or outside the circle x2+y2=100x² + y² = 100?

Tap a statement, then tap the group it belongs in. Then press Check.

Algebra · circles on a grid

The tangent at a point (Higher)

  • A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
  • The radius from O(0,0)O(0, 0) to P(a,b)P(a, b) has gradient ab​b/a.
  • So the tangent at PP has gradient −ba​−a/b, the negative reciprocal.
  • Substitute PP into y=mx+cy = mx + c to find cc.
Worked example Algebra · circles on a grid

Equation of a tangent (Higher)

Question
Find the equation of the tangent to x2+y2=25x² + y² = 25 at the point (3,4)(3, 4).
  1. 1
    Gradient of the radius to (3,4)(3, 4): 34​4/3
  2. 2
    Tangent gradient, the negative reciprocal: −43​−3/4
  3. 3
    Substitute (3,4)(3, 4) into y=−43​x+cy = −3/4x + c: 4=−49​+c4 = −9/4 + c, so c=425​c = 25/4
  4. 4
    Multiply by 4 to clear fractions: 4y=−3x+254y = −3x + 25
Answer
y=−43​x+425​y = −3/4x + 25/4, or 3x+4y=253x + 4y = 25
⚠️ Watch out
the radius gradient 34​4/3 is not the tangent gradient. Flip it and change the sign.
Quick check
?The point (−2,4)(−2, 4) lies on x2+y2=20x² + y² = 20. What is the gradient of the tangent at (−2,4)(−2, 4)?
Calculate
?The point (1,3)(1, 3) lies on the circle x2+y2=10x² + y² = 10. The tangent to the circle at (1,3)(1, 3) crosses the xx-axis at QQ. Find the xx-coordinate of QQ.
Calculate
?The line y=x+1y = x + 1 meets the circle x2+y2=25x² + y² = 25 at two points. Find the positive xx-coordinate of the points of intersection.
Mission check

?A sprinkler at the origin sprays a circle of radius 13 m. Is the plant at (12,6)(12, 6) inside, on or outside the wet circle?

The wet edge is the circle x2+y2=132=169x² + y² = 13² = 169. For the plant, 122+62=18012² + 6² = 180, which is more than 169, so it is outside: about 180​≈13.4√180 ≈ 13.4 m from the sprinkler. It stays dry, even though both coordinates are less than 13.

Recap

Big ideas

  • Place value: each column is 10 times the next; compare decimals column by column, and on a number line further right is bigger.
  • Negatives: same signs multiply or divide to a positive; subtracting a negative adds.
  • Brackets, then powers and roots, then ×× and ÷÷ left to right, then ++ and −− left to right.
  • Binary uses column values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … and only the digits 0 and 1.
  • Factors divide into a number; multiples are in its times table; a prime has exactly two factors (so 1 is not prime).
  • Every whole number above 1 has one prime factor decomposition; write it in index form.
  • HCF: shared primes (the Venn overlap). LCM: all the primes in the Venn diagram. "Next time together" problems need the LCM; "biggest equal groups" problems need the HCF.
  • Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number; simplify using the HCF.
  • Add and subtract with a common denominator; never add the denominators.
  • Multiply tops and bottoms; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
  • Fraction to decimal: divide. Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100. To order, change everything to decimals.
  • A fraction in simplest form terminates only if its denominator's prime factors are 2s and 5s; otherwise it recurs. Every recurring decimal is an exact fraction.
  • Higher: recurring decimal to fraction by multiplying by a power of 10 and subtracting.
  • Higher: Rational numbers can be written as ba​a/b; irrational ones (2​√2, ππ) cannot.
  • An index counts repeated multiplication; a root undoes a power.
  • Same base: multiply → add indices, divide → subtract, power of a power → multiply. a0=1a⁰ = 1 and a−n=an1​a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
  • Higher: anm​=(na​)ma^(m/n) = (n√a)^m. Take the root first.
  • Standard form is A×10nA × 10ⁿ with 1≤A<101 ≤ A < 10; the power counts how far the point moves.
  • Multiply: multiply the numbers, add the powers. Divide: divide, subtract. Add or subtract: match the powers first.
  • Always finish by adjusting AA back into the range 1≤A<101 ≤ A < 10.
  • Round to d.p. or s.f. only at the end; estimate by rounding every number to 1 s.f.
  • A rounded value stands for a range: half a unit below (included) up to half a unit above (not included).
  • Higher: for the largest result, pick upper bounds for what you add or multiply and lower bounds for what you subtract or divide by.
  • A surd such as 2​√2 is an exact irrational root. a​×b​=ab​√a × √b = √ab, but a​+b​=a+b​√a + √b ≠ √(a+b).
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor, then collect like surds.
  • Rationalise a​k​k/(√a) by multiplying top and bottom by a​√a.
  • List systematically: fix one choice, run through the others, then move on; use a table or grid for two choices.
  • Higher: product rule: multiply the number of choices at each stage; reduce the choices when items can't repeat, and do restricted positions first.
  • When order doesn't matter (A v B is the same match as B v A), divide out the double counting.
  • Simplify a ratio by dividing every part by the HCF, after putting the quantities in the same units.
  • Sharing: add the parts, find one part, then multiply. If you know one share or a difference, start from that number of parts instead.
  • A ratio links to fractions of the whole (53​3/5 and 52​2/5) and to a straight line through the origin.
  • Every percentage change is a multiplier: ×1.15× 1.15 for a 15% increase, ×0.85× 0.85 for a 15% decrease. Two changes in a row multiply.
  • Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, times 100.
  • Higher: in a reverse percentage problem, divide the new amount by the multiplier.
  • Repeated percentage change means multiplying by the multiplier once per time period: A=P×mnA = P × mⁿ.
  • Compound interest earns interest on interest; simple interest is the same every year.
  • Use each year's multiplier in turn when the rate changes, and never add the percentages.
  • Direct proportion: both multiply by the same factor; graph is a straight line through the origin; y=kxy = kx.
  • Inverse proportion: the product stays the same; double one, halve the other; y=xk​y = k/x.
  • Higher: for powers and roots, write y=kx2y = kx², y=x2k​y = k/x², y=kx​y = k√x, …, find kk from one pair of values, then use the equation.
  • Area units use the length factor squared; volume units use it cubed. 1 m3=1,000,000 cm3=10001 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1000 litres.
  • Compound measures are rates: speed =timedistance​= distance/time, density =volumemass​= mass/volume, pressure =areaforce​= force/area.
  • Change hours and minutes to decimal hours before dividing, and give the units of your answer.
  • Best value: compare the same unit (price per gram, per litre, per cm²) after converting units.
  • Recipes, exchange rates and map scales are all direct proportion: find the multiplier, and divide to go back.
  • When lengths double, areas multiply by 4: compare pizzas, maps and floor plans by area.
  • Collect only like terms (same letters, same powers); expand by multiplying every term in one bracket by every term in the other.
  • (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², never just a2+b2a² + b²: the grid shows the two missing strips.
  • Factorising undoes expanding: common factor first, then look for x2+bx+cx² + bx + c or a difference of two squares, and check by expanding.
  • Substitute with brackets round negatives, then follow the order of operations.
  • Change the subject by undoing operations in reverse order; if the subject appears twice, collect those terms and factorise.
  • An equation is true for some values, an identity (≡≡) for every value, and a formula links quantities.
  • Expand brackets, collect the unknown on one side, and keep the equation balanced; check by substituting.
  • To compare two deals, write each as an expression, set them equal, and interpret what happens either side of the solution.
  • Inequalities solve like equations, except that multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the sign.
  • Gradient = change in yy ÷ change in xx; in y=mx+cy = mx + c, mm is the gradient and (0,c)(0, c) the yy-intercept.
  • To find a line's equation: gradient first, then substitute a point to find cc.
  • Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular gradients multiply to −1−1 (Higher).
  • Midpoint: average the coordinates. Length: Pythagoras on the changes in xx and yy.
  • Make one side 0, factorise, and set each bracket to 0: each bracket gives a root.
  • Higher: if it will not factorise, use x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a.
  • A quadratic graph can cross a line twice, so a quadratic equation can have two solutions.
  • Two unknowns need two equations; the solution fits both and is where their graphs intersect.
  • Eliminate by matching coefficients and adding or subtracting; substitute when one equation gives y=…y = ….
  • Higher: for a line and a curve, substitute to get a quadratic, then find a yy for each xx.
  • The highest power of xx and its sign set the shape: line, parabola, S-shaped cubic, or two-branch reciprocal.
  • Roots are where y=0y = 0; to solve f(x)=kf(x) = k from a graph, read off where the line y=ky = k meets the curve.
  • Higher/Extended: y=kxy = k^x passes through (0,1)(0, 1) and never touches the xx-axis.
  • A linear sequence adds the same amount each time; its nth term is (difference)×n× n + adjustment.
  • A geometric sequence multiplies by the same amount each time, so it grows much faster.
  • Higher/Extended: constant second differences mean a quadratic nth term; the n2n² coefficient is half the second difference.
  • Gradient of a distance–time graph = speed; steeper means faster; a crossing means the same place at the same time.
  • A straight-line graph's gradient is a rate (km per mile, £ per hour); its intercept is a fixed amount.
  • Higher/Extended: the tangent's gradient gives the rate of change at an instant.
  • Factorise first, then cancel whole factors; never cancel single terms.
  • Add or subtract algebraic fractions over a common denominator, and multiply every term by it to solve an equation.
  • A circle with centre the origin and radius rr has equation x2+y2=r2x² + y² = r²; compare x2+y2x² + y² with r2r² to test a point.
  • The tangent at PP is perpendicular to the radius OPOP: use the negative reciprocal of the radius gradient.
  • To find where a line meets the circle, substitute the line into x2+y2=r2x² + y² = r² and solve the quadratic.
